questions.q: Rutherford famously compared the backscattering result to firing a fifteen-inch naval shell at tissue paper and having it bounce back. What made this so shocking under the accepted model of the day?
options: The alpha particles were expected to be absorbed by the gold, not pass through it
The plum pudding model's soft, diffuse positive charge could only nudge a fast, heavy alpha particle by a fraction of a degree, so a near-180° bounce should have been effectively impossible
The gold foil was far too thick for any particle to pass through at all
Alpha particles were thought to be negatively charged and so should have been attracted, not repelled
questions.explanation: In Thomson's plum pudding atom the positive charge is smeared thinly across the whole atom, so it could only give the heavy, fast alpha particle the tiniest deflection. Turning one completely around required something the model said was not there — a concentrated, dense charge.

questions.q: Which statement best describes Thomson's 'plum pudding' (uniform sphere) model of the atom?
options: A tiny dense positive nucleus at the centre with electrons orbiting in empty space
Positive charge spread smoothly through the whole volume of the atom, with tiny negative electrons dotted throughout it
A solid indivisible ball of neutral matter with no internal structure
Equal numbers of protons and neutrons packed into a central core surrounded by an electron shell
questions.explanation: Thomson pictured the positive charge as the soft 'dough' filling the whole atom, with the light electrons scattered through it like plums. Crucially there was nothing hard, dense or concentrated at the centre — the atom was soft and uniform all the way through.

questions.q: In the Geiger-Marsden experiment, why did the overwhelming majority of alpha particles pass straight through the gold foil with barely any deflection?
options: The gold foil was thin enough that most particles missed all the atoms
Most of the atom is empty space, so most alpha particles travel through the void nowhere near the tiny nucleus and barely feel a force
Gold atoms have no positive charge to deflect the alpha particles
The alpha particles were moving too fast for any force to act on them
questions.explanation: The nuclear model explains this: the atom is almost entirely empty space, so the vast majority of alpha particles sail through the void far from any nucleus and are barely deflected. That most particles pass straight through is the evidence the atom is mostly empty.

questions.q: What force caused the rare alpha particles to be flung almost straight back towards the source?
options: Gravitational attraction between the alpha particle and the gold nucleus
The electrostatic (Coulomb) repulsion between the positive alpha particle and the concentrated positive nucleus, which grows enormous as they approach head-on
Magnetic deflection from the moving charges
Collisions with the electrons spread through the atom
questions.explanation: Both the alpha particle and the nucleus are positive, so they repel via the Coulomb force. On a near head-on approach the repulsion grows stronger the closer they get, decelerating the alpha particle, halting it, and flinging it back the way it came.

questions.q: Roughly what fraction of alpha particles were deflected by more than 90° when fired at the thin gold foil — the figure quoted in the textbook?
options: About 1 in 100
About 1 in 8000
About 1 in 2
About 1 in 10 million
questions.explanation: The team measured roughly one alpha particle in every eight thousand being deflected by more than 90°. That tiny-but-non-zero fraction is what signalled a small, dense, concentrated target inside the atom.

questions.q: After 1911, why was Rutherford's nuclear (planetary) model NOT immediately accepted, despite explaining the gold foil results?
options: It could not explain why most alpha particles passed straight through

Classical electromagnetism (Maxwell) said an orbiting electron is always accelerating, so it must continuously radiate energy, spiral inward, and crash into the nucleus almost instantly — yet matter is stable
It predicted the wrong number of large-angle deflections
Rutherford could not measure the charge of the gold nucleus at all
questions.explanation: By classical physics an accelerating charge radiates energy. An orbiting electron constantly changes direction, so it should radiate, lose energy and spiral into the nucleus in a fraction of a second. Since atoms are clearly stable, the model seemed impossible until Bohr's quantum fix in 1913.

questions.q: From memory: explain how the gold foil observations led to the proposal of the nuclear model of the atom. (This is the exact syllabus 'chain of reasoning' the episode flags for Module 8.)
keyPoints: Most alpha particles passed straight through with little deflection → the atom is mostly empty space.

A tiny fraction (about 1 in 8000) were deflected by more than 90°, and a few bounced almost straight back → the positive charge and nearly all the mass must be concentrated in a tiny, dense central nucleus.
Only a concentrated positive charge could repel a fast, heavy alpha particle so violently — the smeared-out plum pudding model could not.
Therefore the atom has a small dense positive nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space.
questions.explanation: If you linked 'most pass through → mostly empty' and 'rare big bounces → tiny dense positive nucleus', and noted the plum pudding model fails, grade yourself Good or Easy.

questions.q: From memory: what were the alpha particles, the source, and the detection method used in the experiment?
keyPoints: An alpha particle is a helium nucleus: positive charge of +2, mass about 4 atomic units, travelling at roughly 16 million m/s (about 5% of the speed of light).
The source was a strongly radioactive substance referred to as radium C (in modern terms bismuth-214).
Detection used a zinc sulphide screen: each alpha particle striking it produced a single faint flash (a scintillation) counted by eye through a microscope in a darkened room.
The gold foil was extremely thin (about 100 nm, roughly 1000 atoms thick) so each particle passed through as few atoms as possible.
questions.explanation: Reward yourself for the helium nucleus identity (+2 charge, mass 4), the zinc sulphide scintillation screen, and the very thin gold foil. These details are commonly asked in exams.

questions.q: The alpha particles left the source at roughly 16 million m/s. Express this as a percentage of the speed of light (c = 3.0 × 10⁸ m/s), to confirm the episode's '5% of the speed of light' claim.
questions.explanation: Dividing the alpha speed by c gives about 0.053, i.e. roughly 5% of the speed of light — matching the figure stated in the episode. This is why alpha particles count as fast, heavy projectiles.

questions.q: Using the episode's figures, estimate how many times larger the diameter of a gold atom (about 1.5 × 10⁻¹⁰ m) is than the upper limit on the nucleus size (about 10 femtometres = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴ m).
working: \(\text{ratio} \approx 15\,000\) — i.e. the nucleus is at least about 10 000 times smaller than the atom.
questions.explanation: The atom is roughly 10⁴ times wider than its nucleus — the basis for the 'marble in a sports stadium' analogy and the conclusion that the atom is about 99.999...% empty space.
